articles.title: Reddit trao thêm quyền cho AI: Có thể tự động xóa bài viết và bình luận vi phạm nội quy
articles.text:
Reddit đang mở rộng vai trò của AI trong việc kiểm duyệt nội dung với hệ thống Rules Hub. Công cụ mới có thể tự động phát hiện, báo cáo hoặc xóa bài viết, bình luận nếu bị cho là vi phạm quy định của từng cộng đồng.
Reddit vừa giới thiệu Rules Hub, hệ thống kiểm duyệt mới sử dụng mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn (LLM) nhằm hỗ trợ các quản trị viên (moderator) quản lý nội dung trên nền tảng. Điểm đáng chú ý là AI không chỉ gắn cờ nội dung mà còn có thể tự động xóa bài viết hoặc bình luận nếu được moderator cho phép.
Trước đây, Reddit chủ yếu dựa vào đội ngũ moderator tình nguyện cùng công cụ Automoderator (Automod). Hệ thống này hoạt động dựa trên các quy tắc do moderator thiết lập, tự động kích hoạt khi phát hiện từ khóa hoặc mẫu nội dung nhất định.
Trong thời gian qua, Reddit đã từng bước đưa AI vào quy trình kiểm duyệt. Một ví dụ là tính năng Post Check, sử dụng mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn để cảnh báo người dùng khi nội dung nháp có nguy cơ vi phạm quy định của cộng đồng, nhưng vẫn cho phép họ đăng bài nếu muốn.
Với Rules Hub, AI được giao thêm quyền hạn. Theo thông tin được The Verge đăng tải đầu tiên, hệ thống mới có khả năng đánh giá liệu một bài viết hoặc bình luận có "phù hợp với tinh thần của một quy định" hay không, thay vì chỉ tìm kiếm các từ khóa cố định như Automod.
Reddit cho biết cách tiếp cận này giúp AI hiểu tốt hơn ngôn ngữ tự nhiên, ngữ cảnh cũng như những trường hợp đặc biệt không chứa chính xác các từ khóa đã được thiết lập trong quy tắc.
Dù vậy, moderator vẫn là người quyết định AI sẽ thực thi những quy định nào và hành động ra sao khi phát hiện nội dung có dấu hiệu vi phạm. Các lựa chọn hiện bao gồm báo cáo để con người xem xét, tự động xóa nội dung hoặc không thực hiện bất kỳ hành động nào.
Theo Reddit, Rules Hub đã được thử nghiệm trong vài tháng qua trên hơn 700 cộng đồng, với sự tham gia của cả các moderator mới lẫn nhiều moderator giàu kinh nghiệm, bao gồm các thành viên thuộc Mod Council Network.
Hiện công cụ này được triển khai mặc định cho tất cả subreddit mới được tạo. Reddit cho biết sẽ mở rộng Rules Hub tới toàn bộ nền tảng trong năm 2026, nhưng chưa công bố thời điểm cụ thể.
Những phản hồi ban đầu từ moderator vẫn còn khá trái chiều. Một người tham gia thử nghiệm nhận xét hiệu quả của hệ thống "lúc được lúc không", trong khi một moderator khác cho biết nhóm của họ chưa đủ tin tưởng để AI tự động xử lý nội dung mà chỉ sử dụng nó như công cụ gắn cờ phục vụ việc kiểm tra thủ công.
Về lâu dài, Reddit cho biết Rules Hub có thể thay thế nhiều tác vụ mà Automod đang đảm nhiệm khi kết hợp cùng các công cụ Post and Comment Guidance và Safety Filters. Tuy nhiên, công ty nhấn mạnh AI không thay thế moderator. Con người vẫn sẽ chịu trách nhiệm xây dựng quy định của cộng đồng, cấu hình hệ thống và xem xét các quyết định do AI đưa ra.
Động thái này được đưa ra chỉ vài tháng sau khi Reddit vấp phải phản ứng từ cộng đồng moderator vì thay đổi chính sách, hạn chế khả năng để các bot tự động cấm người dùng chỉ dựa trên hoạt động của họ ở những subreddit khác.

articles.title: Flock Highlighted Police Departments Using Its Tech. Now 4 Face Allegations of Misuse
articles.text:
Flock, the increasingly controversial automatic license plate reader (ALPR) company, has previously highlighted at least four police departments on its YouTube page that have since faced allegations of misusing the company’s technology.
The company featured the Savannah Police Department in a March 2022 YouTube video. Four officers and two workers from the department were recently placed on administrative leave after an internal investigation found “potential misuses” of Flock’s ALPR system. Also in Georgia, the Albany Police Department was the subject of a glossy 2024 video. Five officers from the department were recently arrested and charged in connection to their alleged misuse of the technology.
Flock also highlighted the Sandy Springs Police Department in a 2020 video about how the company was helping police combat so-called porch pirates. Last year, a Sandy Springs Police Department officer was terminated amid an internal investigation into alleged misuse of Flock’s technology. The Baytown Police Department was featured in Flock’s 2025 video about responding to a carjacking; last week, a Baytown police officer resigned amid ongoing investigations into alleged misuse of the technology.
Allegations of ALPR misuse have plagued police departments across the country, including in states like Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, and Wisconsin. In Georgia alone—home to the Savannah, Albany, and Sandy Springs police departments—allegations of ALPR misuse have also been reported at the sheriff’s offices of Coweta County, Cherokee County, Habersham County, and Richmond County.
While these incidents show that police departments have mechanisms to detect and address ALPR misuse, Flock's promotional materials show that it can occur even at departments that were touted as exemplary.
| Got a Tip? | 
|---|
| Are you a current or former Flock employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61. | 
In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel emphasized that “misuse was identified and addressed.” He said that incidents of misuse shouldn’t discount Flock’s usefulness to police departments.
“That is exactly why accountability tools and internal review processes exist,” Lewbel said in an emailed statement. “When improper use is detected, agencies can investigate, take action, and hold individuals accountable. That should be viewed as evidence that oversight mechanisms are working, not as a sign that the entire department or city should be broadly condemned.”
The Flock YouTube channel’s video about the Albany Police Department features interviews with senior crime and intelligence analyst David Sparks, whom Flock recognized as a “Power Partner” in 2024, and chief Michael J. Persley. In it, Sparks describes Flock as a crucial tool for fighting “property crime” and “crimes of opportunity.”
“To ensure that the community trusts us, there are a lot of things we have to do, and the first part of building that trust is open, honest transparency and communication,” Persley says in the video. “So I'm not trying to listen to your conversations, I'm not trying to see what's happening in your backyard. We wanna make sure that you're safe.”
On July 6, the Albany Police Department announced that it had fired five officers following an internal investigation into "serious policy violations involving the improper use" of ALPRs. The police department said that three of these officers were fired for improper use of ALPRs, while the other two were fired for “separate, unrelated policy violations uncovered during the administrative investigation.” The Georgia Bureau of Investigation charged the officers for misuse of license plate data and violating their oaths of office.
The Albany Police Department did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Flock’s Savannah video centers on an interview with then major of police Robert Gavin, who praised how Flock facilitates data-sharing between different law enforcement agencies.
“We spent a lot of time doing community talks about what we're gonna use them for, what we're not gonna use them for,” Gavin says, adding that the overall objective is to “keep everybody safe.”
On July 31, Savannah police mayor Van Johnson wrote in a Facebook post that the allegations involving the six employees had been referred to the GBI to determine whether criminal charges should be filed.
The Savannah Police Department did not respond for comment. The GBI confirmed that it investigated the incidents in Savannah and Albany, but didn’t provide information, noting that the Savannah investigation is “still active.”
According to Johnson, the Savannah Police Department conducted an internal investigation through the Flock Safety Audit Assistance Program, which Flock introduced in April. In a press release announcing the tool, Flock said it “continuously monitors system activity and surfaces search patterns that fall outside an agency’s typical usage.” Savannah police chief Lenny Gunther told a local news outlet that the investigation surfaced 127 inappropriate searches out of the 39,000 it conducted this year.
“Public trust is non-negotiable,” Johnson said in his Facebook statement. “These tools exist to keep our community safe, not for personal or unauthorized use.”
In 2020, Flock posted a video by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution about the Sandy Springs Police Department’s arrest of a porch pirate. The video did not feature any interviews with Sandy Springs Police Department personnel, but noted that the man was arrested after a Flock camera captured the license plate of the suspect.
About five years later, the Sandy Springs Police Department launched an internal investigation into whether one of its officers had misused Flock’s technology. According to investigators, the officer allegedly ran ALPR searches to support beta testing for Signal 8, a law enforcement software company that employed the officer in a second job.
This officer, the police department claimed, did not cooperate with its investigation and was subsequently terminated.
Meanwhile, Flock showcased the Baytown Police Department in 2025 as part of a brief series highlighting cases where police said Flock was instrumental in apprehending a suspect.
“We use it multiple times every day, and once I log in to my computer, Flock is the first thing I click on,” a Baytown police officer says.
On July 30, Baytown police chief John Stringer announced the resignation of a police officer who had been under investigation for allegedly misusing Flock’s technology. The Baytown Police Department did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
In his video statement, Stringer said that two investigations into the officer’s alleged misuse—one internal, one criminal—remained ongoing.
“Accountability to the fullest extent of the law will be pursued,” Stringer added.

articles.title: Một điểm chạm Tammi: Giải mã nỗi đau quá tải ứng dụng với nền tảng hội tụ mới của Viettel
articles.text:
Trong khi smartphone của bạn đang bị quá tải với hàng loạt ứng dụng riêng lẻ khác nhau, Viettel đã tìm ra cách giải quyết triệt để vấn đề này.
Trong đời sống số hiện đại, chiếc smartphone của mỗi người đang rơi vào tình trạng "quá tải" khi phải cài đặt hàng loạt ứng dụng riêng lẻ. Muốn theo dõi camera an ninh tại nhà phải mở một ứng dụng, kiểm tra hành trình đơn hàng chuyển phát nhanh phải cài một ứng dụng khác, rồi lại cần thêm các phần mềm riêng để tra cứu dịch vụ thu phí không dừng, ký số hay quản lý cước di động.
Sự phân mảnh này không chỉ chiếm dụng dung lượng bộ nhớ mà còn tiêu tốn không ít thời gian, công sức ghi nhớ mật khẩu và thao tác của người dùng. Để giải quyết triệt để "nỗi đau" đó, Viettel đã tích hợp toàn bộ dịch vụ của Viettel vào nền tảng Viettel Tammi, biến ứng dụng này thành một điểm chạm duy nhất khám phá trọn vẹn hệ sinh thái dịch vụ Viettel.
Từ sự phân mảnh lộn xộn đến một trải nghiệm liền mạch
Trước đây, hệ sinh thái sản phẩm và dịch vụ đa dạng của Tập đoàn Viettel được vận hành trên nhiều nền tảng ứng dụng khác nhau. Dù giúp chuyên môn hóa từng dịch vụ, mô hình này cũng có hạn chế khi khách hàng phải chuyển đổi liên tục giữa các icon trên màn hình.
Với sự xuất hiện của MyViettel trên Tammi, từ duy quản lý rời rạc đã chính thức nhường chỗ cho mô hình chăm sóc khách hàng hợp nhất. Khách hàng chỉ cần sử dụng một tài khoản đăng nhập duy nhất để theo dõi và điều khiển toàn bộ các dịch vụ Viettel mà mình đang đứng tên:
Quản lý đa tài khoản, đa dịch vụ tập trung: Từ các thuê bao di động chính chủ, Internet cố định, Truyền hình cho đến Home Camera, chữ ký số MySign... tất cả đều hiển thị trên một giao diện trực quan để khách hàng quản lý tổng thể về dịch vụ và các tài khoản.
Thay thế các ứng dụng vệ tinh: Người dùng có thể xem trực tiếp hình ảnh từ Home Camera mà không cần cài đặt ứng dụng Viettel Home. Thực hiện đăng ký và ký số tức thì mà không cần mở ứng dụng MySign. Đặt chuyến, theo dõi hành trình bưu gửi Viettel Post, thanh toán tiền bằng Viettel Money hay kiểm tra lịch sử qua trạm ePass ngay tại một màn hình duy nhất.
Nâng cao trải nghiệm khách hàng: Mỗi khách hàng sẽ có một nhân viên chăm sóc khách hàng đồng hành, hỗ trợ 24/7. Các công nghệ được ứng dụng nhằm cá nhân hóa dịch vụ cho khách hàng đồng thời hỗ trợ khách hàng giải quyết vấn đề một cách nhanh chóng: hay tắt/bật modem wifi từ xa, báo lỗi dịch vụ cho trợ lý cá nhân,….
Một tài khoản, một ứng dụng, một điểm chạm – đó không chỉ là sự thay đổi về mặt giao diện của một ứng dụng, mà là bước chuyển mình quan trọng trong chiến lược lấy khách hàng làm trung tâm của Viettel.
Bằng việc tích hợp toàn bộ dịch vụ về Viettel Tammi, Viettel không chỉ trả lại sự thảnh thơi, tinh gọn cho chiếc điện thoại của người dùng, mà còn mở ra cánh cửa kết nối liền mạch, an toàn và gắn kết hơn giữa nhà mạng với từng hộ gia đình Việt.
KHÁCH HÀNG CÓ THỂ LÀM GÌ TRÊN MY VIETTEL CỦA TAMMI?
• ✔️ Giao tiếp & Di động: Quản lý toàn bộ các số điện thoại di động chính chủ, tra cứu cước sử dụng và thanh toán cước tập trung.
• ✔️ Viễn thông cố định: Quản lý đường truyền Internet cố định và dịch vụ Truyền hình trên cùng một tài khoản.
• ✔️ Giám sát an ninh: Xem trực tiếp Home Camera mà không cần cài ứng dụng Viettel Home.
• ✔️ Chữ ký số: Đăng ký và thực hiện ký số MySign trực tiếp ngay trên Tammi.
• ✔️ Giao thông thông minh: Tra cứu thông tin ePass (lịch sử qua trạm, tài khoản giao thông...).
• ✔️ Logistics: Đặt đơn và theo dõi hành trình bưu gửi Viettel Post trên cùng một ứng dụng.
• ✔️ Thanh toán tích hợp: Thanh toán cước cho nhiều dịch vụ và nhiều thuê bao cùng lúc chỉ với một lần thao tác.

articles.title: ICE’s DNA Collection Increases, SpaceX’s Rocket Crashes Into the Moon, and the AI Backlash Grows
articles.text:
This week on Uncanny Valley, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down how ICE has collected DNA from nearly a million people this year, including young children, feeding an FBI database indefinitely. The team also discusses the backlash against Google Earth’s AI slop, the White House’s secretive AI cybersecurity plan, and a SpaceX rocket crashing into the moon. Plus, WIRED’s Molly Taft discusses their recent story on the strange left-right coalition fighting data centers across the US.
Articles mentioned in this episode:
You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @Zoëschiffer, Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger, and Molly Taft on Bluesky @mollytaft.com. Write to us at [email protected].
How to Listen
You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:
If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.
Transcript
Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.
Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.
Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.
Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.
Brian Barrett: Today on the show, we're talking about how the Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agency, better known as ICE, has been collecting DNA samples at an alarming rate. These samples have led to hundreds of thousands of people, including young children, to end up in an FBI criminal database basically forever.
Zoë Schiffer: We'll also get into one of our favorite topics, AI slop. From Google Earth disabling its new AI tool after people used it to create fake maps to Substack partnering with the AI writing detection tool Pangram, companies are starting to realize that people really don't like low-quality AI content flooding their feeds.
Leah Feiger: Also in the realm of AI, the White House announced a plan to tackle the increasing security risks brought on by AI companies. It's keeping the details mostly under wraps, but we're going to discuss what's behind all the secrecy and what this could mean for future regulation.
Brian Barrett: We'll also talk about how part of a SpaceX rocket crashed into the moon, leaving a new crater behind and all kinds of questions.
Leah Feiger: And later in the show, WIRED senior writer Molly Taft joins to tell us all about how data centers have officially broken US politics.
Brian Barrett: Well, to start off, let's talk about ICE, which we haven't in a little bit, but they're still there. They're still doing bad things, including collecting DNA samples. WIRED’s Dhruv Mehrotra reported this week about how ICE has collected nearly 1 million people's DNA this past year, just this past year alone, including that of young children. As we mentioned up top, this DNA collection has led to hundreds of thousands of people with no criminal convictions ending up in an FBI database indefinitely. And in fact, the Department of Homeland Security has become the single largest source of new profiles in this database.
Leah Feiger: I feel like we're getting inundated with here's one more part of your privacy, here's one more part of security, here's one more bit of immigrants being treated as subhuman. But this one, at least enough for me, broke through the noise. Don't you guys think? This was wild.
Zoë Schiffer: I feel like I have a question before we move forward, which is maybe one that's shared by listeners. Why is DNA being collected from immigrants in the first place? This surprised me, and maybe I'm a little naïve about what they're subjected to when they're in this country.
Brian Barrett: Yeah, I mean, I think the answer is because they can. And I wish that we're more nuanced or subtle than that, but I think they are just trying to gather as much information as they can at all times. I want to be clear too, these are not people with criminal convictions, people who are even necessarily suspected of a crime. It is just such a wide net that they are casting. In fact, internal training materials that drove, in partnership with researchers at Georgetown, we should say, dug up, said that asylum seekers and refugees who have not adjusted their immigration status must have their DNA sampled and that the DNA needs to be collected after any arrest. It is just table stakes for these officers to grab DNA whenever and wherever they can.
Leah Feiger: And already a lot of lawmakers have been speaking out against this. For example, when learning that children were being swabbed at a family detention center in Dilley, Texas, a number of representatives said in a joint statement to WIRED, none of the families at Dilley have been convicted of a crime. They do not belong in a database meant for violent criminals, especially children. This is starting to pick up steam across the board. I think that we've just gotten so used to the idea that the government is allowed to collect any information it wants, store it in whichever way it wants. And all of these norms have been destroyed in the last year and a half. It's really shocking, honestly.
Zoë Schiffer: So you're saying basically that refusing to allow your DNA to be collected can become its own chart, can become a mark on your record regardless of what you had previously.
Brian Barrett: Not only a mark on your record. WIRED and Dhruv identified two prosecutions filed in 2025 against people in immigration custody who refused DNA collection. It is becoming a crime to say, "I don't want you to do that." That's one thing. Then the other thing too that I think we've mentioned, but I want to dig into a little bit, is that they have started recently... I think the shift to collecting DNA from families is also relatively new. And we're talking about, I think the official line is that kids as young as 14 can have their DNA collected, but Georgetown and WIRED identified 492 children under 14 whose DNA the agency sent to the FBI, not just collected, but sent onto the FBI between January 2025 and January 2026. That included 21 5-year-olds, 32 6-year-olds, 33 7-year-olds who are now in an FBI DNA database for the rest of their lives.
Leah Feiger: I mean, the kicker to me here too, part of this has to do with "preventing future crime." It's all supposed to be about how the primary purpose is to build a national DNA database for solving crimes, which is a theory. OK, sure. Solving crimes, cool about that. But these are 5-year-olds. These are 5-year-olds whose—so many of their rights have already been taken away by this current administration and DOJ and DHS. To have that as an additional marker to me is a really important visual next step of the war on immigrants at this moment in the country.
Zoë Schiffer: All right. I'm going to take us from the depths of despair. Just drag us up.
Brian Barrett: Some would say AI slop is maybe not the depths, but we're definitely still in despair territory.
Leah Feiger: I mean, I love the depths of despair, my favorite place to be.
Zoë Schiffer: I find it funny, but I have a bunch of thoughts on it and my views on this have been evolving really rapidly, so I'm excited to talk to you about it.
Leah Feiger: Good, good, good, good.
Zoë Schiffer: Last week, Google rolled out a new AI feature on Google Earth, which would basically let anyone zoom into real coordinates on a map and type a prompt just like you would in ChatGPT or Gemini and superimpose an AI scene on top of real Google satellite imagery.
Brian Barrett: What could go wrong?
Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I have a hard time imagining how no one during this process said, "This is a terrible idea," or perhaps they did and they were not listened to. But regardless, Google did this. As you might imagine, it took 24 hours for people to generate fabricated nuclear plants in Iran, a bombed hospital in Gaza, and fires at an Iranian oil terminal. People were extremely upset about this for misinformation, disinformation, and other reasons, and Google quickly disabled the feature. It just feels like there is a real split between how Silicon Valley feels about AI and uses AI and how the rest of the country feels about it and uses it, because these tools are pretty unpopular, even as they're being widely adopted. But I think that the way that they're being adopted is also really different. Most people are using ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude as basically a replacement for Google. Whereas in Silicon Valley, they're using it as a replacement for a personal assistant or a junior employee. And so for them, I think there is real magic in the tools and the capabilities. But for everyone else, the thing you hear a lot is why is this being shoved down our throats? We don't want this. They're stuffing AI features in all of these apps that we previously used and were good, and the AI features are bad.
Brian Barrett: Well, I think it's AI slop specifically, right? Yeah, there are use cases for AI agents. Zoë, you've given over some percentage of your life to them already. It's working out great for you. But what I find interesting about this is (A) how quickly they rolled it back, and (B) it's just the latest in a series of steps like this where companies that have been sort of embracing AI up to this point are acknowledging through actual feature changes to their products that, hey, maybe people don't like this. Just in the last week or so, you had LinkedIn adding a little button to a post where you can say, "I think this looks like AI slop. I don't like this." LinkedIn, which has basically been a platform that has been built the last year or so on saying, "Hey, look at all the AI slop you can make on this platform." That's their whole thing.
Zoë Schiffer: Love AI slop.
Brian Barrett: But now they're saying, OK, we can actually give people a chance to say no. You had a couple of weeks ago, Substack, in the app, you can check to see if it's potentially AI generated. They partnered with a company called Pangram, which is a very good AI detector tool. Again, Substack, a company that has said in the past, "Hey, if people want to use AI, that's great." And then more broadly outside of companies themselves, if I can monologue slightly longer because I'm passionate about this.
Zoë Schiffer: No, please go. Go off.
Brian Barrett: The EU on Sunday, a new regulation kicked in that said, "Look, anytime you come across AI slop in your feed, whatever it is, it has to be labeled as AI slop. Every piece of AI content has to be labeled as such," which is a huge sea change for people over there. If you're an AI creator, if you're just someone on social media, it's telling that, yeah, people want to know when they're seeing it and they want the option not to see it. And companies are listening.
Zoë Schiffer: It's interesting because I was hearing this a lot from actual AI researchers at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and they were saying it's so annoying how all of our executives are constantly just posting their AI. They won't just post their own messages on Slack. It sounds very distinctive. It's not that it's posting misinformation or getting facts wrong. I think largely the tools really have improved on that front. You need to check them. You need to be literate on that, but it's more that the patterns and the way that they speak is distinctive and there's an ick factor for people. I really am noticing that these days, the difference between an executive who is a good writer and actually saying something that they're passionate about and writing it themselves and posting it on social media, and then someone who very clearly, whatever, maybe they had a conversation with Claude and it's just 100 percent AI-generated output, my eyes glaze over it. It is genuinely hard to read this stuff. It's hard to remember what you just read. I think is getting bigger and bigger. And I think that real human writing, real human output and content is going to be an edge for companies that are willing to invest in it, which is not to say that there isn't cool uses of AI. I actually had a real unlock this week, because nothing unites writers and reporters more than how much we hate our CMSes. I legit just built a better one. It works beautifully. You can post blogs. It took me no time at all. It really was like a, OK, wow, these tools can do amazing things. But that's very, very, very different than what we're talking about with Substack or Google.
Brian Barrett: I want to take a quick moment to flag that Zoë just used unlock as a noun.
Zoë Schiffer: Oh, no.
Leah Feiger: It was painful. Just to be clear, I'm with Brian on this.
Brian Barrett: Yeah. I felt like it was important to say that. And then we'll move on. And then we'll move on.
Zoë Schiffer: I deserve that. You spend too much time in Silicon Valley and you become one.
Leah Feiger: OK. I am game to keep talking about AI, but let's pivot a little bit to the White House, if that's all right with you guys.
Brian Barrett: It is.
Leah Feiger: Great. Great. I feel like we've talked about this, honestly, a bunch, which is the White House is trying to figure out how to regulate AI, specifically keeping in mind cybersecurity risks. We talked about how the Trump administration has had different officials weighing in, how people have had some fun little disagreements. Apparently, as of this week, they have now all arrived at a common framework, and for the most part, they refuse to tell you anything about it.
Zoë Schiffer: Love that.
Leah Feiger: Love that. On Tuesday, the White House brought together staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, and a couple other AI companies to walk through its finalized AI cybersecurity oversight plan. The details of the plan haven't been released publicly, but we do know that developers can voluntarily submit new models up to 30 days ahead of release, and then the government is going to test their hacking capabilities using a classified benchmark. From there, they're going to share the results with federal agencies and "trusted corporate partners." Reportedly, open weight models are being entirely excluded. I feel like I said a lot of details, but honestly, we're not getting a lot of details yet, really, about what's included here. A lot of companies feel like they're being left out. The White House has had some wild quotes about how they do have to keep things classified and even unclassified things they might not be comfortable sharing with the public. It could all be a national security risk, et cetera, which is language we've heard for a very long time. And in many ways, this just keeps a lot of this a bit opaque. I'm really curious what you guys think about any of this.
Brian Barrett: Can I set up some backdrop? The backdrop against which this is happening, which is over the last week and a half or so, we have had a continuing series of revelations and disclosures about how AI models have been escaping their sandboxes, have been going out on the open web, have been hacking companies. A version of Anthropic's Mythos 5, not the same one that's available to the public because it had its security safeguards switched off. Nevertheless, it literally made up online personas to try to trick a GitHub repo manager into accepting a malicious pull request. That's a lot of words just to basically try to social engineer somebody into planting malware. This is all happening very, very fast. It is getting worse very, very quickly. We have a story from Will Knight that he just published on Wednesday about how the next step, which we're not too far off from, is going to be potentially malicious AI models that could get out in the world and self-replicate, turn into viruses, worms. All of which is to say, I think we need to know what the AI security framework is in part to understand just how far short it falls of where it needs to be.
Zoë Schiffer: I mean, yes, and it's voluntary. It's in the name that this field ... I mean, I get that companies will feel compelled to be part of this, but it's unclear to me what this actually does functionally. Are companies going to do this because if they don't, they can't contract with the government. And so we just expect everyone to fall in line. It just feels like it's starting out from such a toothless place. I will say, just before we move on, the Anthropic, OpenAI disclosures on the agent hacking was giving me so much joy last week. OpenAI having its moment in the sun being like, "We are so scary and powerful. We just did a bad thing. Oopsie doopsie." And then Anthropic couldn't let them have it. They're like, "We also investigated, and you know what? Our agents did it too, and maybe it was worse."
Brian Barrett: Also scary.
Leah Feiger: I think something though also that I can't stop thinking about is the White House has left, by virtue of the way that they're doing this, they've left smaller AI startups, safety advocates and a bunch of other researchers, et cetera, very much in the dark of how they're addressing all of these cyber risks. Some people from these companies have argued that this is going to give an advantage to larger companies who actually know what hoops they now have to jump through. Vice versa, maybe some of these other smaller companies are just going to decide not to really jump through those hoops. So we're leaving a lot of gaps here. This is clearly not the comprehensive plan that everyone, I don't know if they were hoping for, but at the very least needed.
Zoë Schiffer: But also aren't open-weight models pretty critical for cybersecurity at this point?
Leah Feiger: Yes.
Zoë Schiffer: I'm just so confused about the rationale for leaving them out.
Leah Feiger: Even I know that. Even I am aware of that.
Brian Barrett: I was just going to say that. Yeah.
Zoë Schiffer: So you know it's legit.
Brian Barrett: One of us. One of us. No, but talk about gaps. That's the biggest potential pain point in the future. I think is going to be super capable open weight models that you can't control, so what's the plan there? And to say, we've got an AI security framework. By the way, we're not going to talk about that.
Leah Feiger: Toothless. It's toothless.
Brian Barrett: Very tooth—yeah. Yep. Before we go to break, let's talk briefly about a SpaceX rocket, part of which crashed into the moon on Wednesday morning. The rocket piece, it was part of SpaceX's Falcon 9. It was carrying a pair of lunar landers that successfully reached the surface some time ago. But as part of that journey, one piece was left to drift because it didn't have enough fuel to return to Earth or to enter a stable orbit. So it's just been hanging out for 18 months, going round and round, looking for a place to land. And it found one Wednesday morning. Slammed into the moon at a speed of 5,400 miles per hour. That is approximately seven times the speed of sound. I don't know if that matters in space, but it is just for context of how fast it is. There are no pictures yet of the impact, but people do think it likely created a new crater on the moon. I mean, that is what moon craters are after all, just space stuff slamming into it at ridiculous speeds. Just this one happened to be sent by Elon Musk. What do we think about space crashes, everybody?
Leah Feiger: I mean, look, there's already so much space trash around. The fact that there's space trash everywhere. Where is this debris going? No, it's just all going to remain in Earth's orbit, and we're going to have to have our descendants deal with this in years to come.
Zoë Schiffer: I have been talking to the astronomer community. I really have to always say, "Zoë, don't say astrologer," because I'm from California and it's just very close to me.
Brian Barrett: And you are talking to both.
Zoë Schiffer: And I'm talking to both at all times. Astronomers are very up in arms precisely because of what you just said, Leah. They feel like there is so much junk up in space now. And SpaceX's plan is to launch a whole bunch more stuff up in space. Makes it really hard to see the night sky. Their telescopes aren't working like they used to. And now we're seeing remains of rockets actually crash into the moon. So yeah, I think they have a point.
Brian Barrett: There's one element to this. Speaking of future generations, NASA does want to build a base on the moon, at least one base. There is a plan. It's why Project Artemis happened. It's why we sent astronauts up around the dark side of it. It's already been a concern that, look, if you build a moon base, how are you going to protect it from various space objects slamming into the moon's surface? The more we send rockets up, the more likely it is that we're just adding new threats. Again, the moon's a big place. The odds that it would hit a specific moon base location, pretty small, but it's something you have to think about. If you really think that that's an achievable mission and a viable path for humanity, how are we going to not get hit on the head with a SpaceX rocket?
Zoë Schiffer: You don't want our big space data center to be taken out by a random piece of SpaceX trash.
Brian Barrett: No.
Zoë Schiffer: Geez.
Brian Barrett: God, that would be poetic though, if a Grok database were taken out by a SpaceX Falcon 9.
Leah Feiger: A reminder that this weekend, like all weekends, is a good time to watch the movie Don't Look Up. If you're looking for recommendations, here's one.
Zoë Schiffer: I really feel like people didn't appreciate that as much as they should've. I thought it was really good.
Leah Feiger: It's really good. I'm forever a big fan. Brian?
Brian Barrett: I did not see it.
Leah Feiger: What?
Brian Barrett: And I don't think I'm going to.
Zoë Schiffer: Coming up after the break, we'll be getting into how data centers broke US politics. Stay with us.
Leah Feiger: Data centers have become one of the only things that pretty much everyone agrees on, including Democrats and Republicans. Over the past year, we've seen moratoriums pass in blue states and deep red counties alike, with attack on pro-data center city councilmen, protestors getting arrested at public meetings from New Jersey to Wisconsin, and so much more. But this movement against data centers holds some really strange origins. WIRED’s Molly Taft spent the last few months investigating some of the different factions within the coalition and their motivations. Molly followed a Steve Bannon–affiliated tech correspondent around Georgia, heard data centers being compared to neurons of the Antichrist, and spoke with Democrats who have been linking arms with right-wing speakers to push against these AI build-outs. Molly, thank you so much for joining us today.
Molly Taft: Thank you so much for having me.
Leah Feiger: To start off, can we just get into how fast the backlash against data centers has actually grown? You talk about a jump from under 100,000 to half a million people in data-center-opposition Facebook groups in the last couple of months. Talk us through that. What changed? How did this go?
Molly Taft: Yeah. Man, I sit up at night thinking about this, to be honest, which is maybe a bad sign. Most data centers in the US before basically two years ago, they were being built outside of DC and Silicon Valley were the two big places. And so there had been a couple of local environmental groups, especially in the DC area, where there were increasingly more and more who were starting to point out some of the environmental issues with this. So when I got to WIRED, those groups had been getting a little bit louder as there were more and more data centers that had started being built. So I started tracking them. But it's been interesting because this is really an area where politicians in Washington were not aware of what was going on at all until it seems like maybe the past six months. People are so mad about this for multiple different reasons. And I remember asking a colleague in the newsroom, "Do you think this could be used to block state-level policies on data centers?" Because there were some states where local lawmakers, again in Virginia, a big one, were starting to be like, "Hey, the power on these things is crazy. They're being built with few restrictions. We need to start talking about regulating these things." There was really not a lot in the 2024, 2025 state legislative agenda. And I remember asking that question, and then two days later, Marjorie Taylor Greene tweeted about it. And I was like, "Oh, yeah, OK. The people who are clocking some of this are not the normal political coalitions that you will see."
Brian Barrett: Molly, you spent a good amount of time with a guy named Joe Allen down in Georgia who is a fascinating character/person who comes at this from the right-wing perspective, which I found that's the most interesting and revelatory to me is why this faction is so opposed to you. Talk about Joe and how you found him and his role in all this.
Molly Taft: Yeah, Joe is a really interesting character, and he comes from another portion of this conversation, which is when people oppose data centers, are they opposing AI in general? Joe was a musical rigger for many years for the Black Eyed Peas, Calvin Harris. He basically helped set up shows all over the world, but he also had this longstanding interest in tech. He's been thinking a lot about what it means to have this global cabal of tech elites control humanity's future. And he got an offer from Steve Bannon to come on War Room and be its anti-tech or its transhumanist editor. That's what it's called. He's been talking about the dangers of AI on War Room for a while. As the mainstream tech and the big tech companies aligned behind Trump, there are a significant faction of MAGA and the populous space that are deeply uncomfortable with what a lot of these companies are representing. And I was like, I got to have some sort of guide as to how the right is coming at tech. I understand how the right comes at some of these environmental issues, but I really want to understand how the tech right thinks about this.
Leah Feiger: OK. Yeah, get into this a little bit more with us. You spoke with a Democrat who has this big environmental science background running the Facebook group, a protester in New Jersey who describes right-wing allies as their temporary allies. Is this an actual durable coalition, an alliance of convenience? I'm really fascinated by this.
Molly Taft: It is. I also think that when I talk to a lot of people on the left, a lot of them are a little bit maybe politically blind to the fact that these ideas are resonating cross-party. I think what's interesting is when folks like the ones working on the ground, specific protesters, this is becoming a really good coalition-building issue. I—actually, this is not in the piece, but I spoke two months ago or so to Will Lawrence, who just won his primary last night. He was the far-left candidate in a Michigan district where there is a lot of data center development, and he really ran on that issue. And he said he was having a lot of really interesting cross-party conversations with people who are just like, "I do not want this here. I don't want it at all."
Zoë Schiffer: No, they definitely don't. I mean, I've been thinking about a couple points when you're talking. One is I think a difference with the clean energy movement and that build out where there was opposition, but there was also a very clear yes coalition. Whereas with AI, and I was talking about this earlier, the way that people in Silicon Valley use AI where it's like it's genuinely doing the work of junior-level employees, it's really changing their day-to-day in a magical and amazing way. And then how the average person uses it where it's not a necessary part of their lives in any way. It's like a lot of people, including probably people that oppose these projects, might use ChatGPT, but it's Google. It's just not a big deal. It doesn't feel like there's this strong coalition of people that are advocating for the data centers, except for the very, very tech elite. And those people are themselves so unpopular that it just feels like this whole issue has become radioactive.
Molly Taft: I think that's such a good point. I also think another thing that differentiates this from the renewable stuff is why I started talking to Joe is that there is this huge almost spiritual question about what are our lives going to look like if this technology is allowed to develop? I think a lot of people aren't directly thinking about that, but you're seeing news about how this is going to take your job and you're seeing news about what are your kids getting exposed to in school? What are your kids' lives going to look like? It's going to be so different from yours if this technology becomes more widespread. There is this really spiritual crisis element to it that I think doesn't necessarily cross everyone's minds, but plays a really important role. And I think that's something that is, I think, going to keep galvanizing people. I've been thinking a lot about what could tech companies do to tamp down some of this opposition? And I don't really know if I have an answer for them because I think even if they're like, "We will pay for everything. We'll make sure it's all connected to renewable energy. You will get an incredible tax base, durable jobs, whatever you want," maybe I'm wrong, I don't really see a lot of instances in which that would still fly for people. I just don't think people want these things at all.
Leah Feiger: Molly, thank you so much for joining us.
Molly Taft: Thank you for having me.
Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact-checked by Matt Giles. Marc Leyda is our San Francisco studio engineer. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

articles.title: Chrome cuối cùng cũng hỗ trợ Netflix 4K, nhưng chỉ cho Windows
articles.text:
Bản cập nhật Google Chrome cho phép người dùng xem được nội dung 4K trên Netflix, tuy nhiên chỉ hỗ trợ cho hệ điều hành Windows.
Netflix vừa cập nhật trang yêu cầu hệ thống, liệt kê Google Chrome bản 117 trở lên là trình duyệt đủ điều kiện phát nội dung Ultra HD 2160p trên Windows. Đây là thay đổi người dùng phát hiện trước, không phải một thông báo chính thức từ Netflix hay Google. Một tài khoản X đăng bằng chứng phát 4K trên Chrome hôm 23/7, sau đó trang FlatPanelsHD và The Mac Observer xác nhận Netflix đã đổi trang hỗ trợ, kéo theo hàng loạt báo công nghệ đưa tin trong tuần đầu tháng 8.
Trước đây, muốn xem Netflix ở độ phân giải cao nhất trên máy tính Windows, người dùng gần như bắt buộc phải mở Microsoft Edge hoặc dùng app Netflix cài từ Microsoft Store. Chrome, dù chiếm thị phần trình duyệt lớn nhất thế giới, lại bị Netflix giới hạn ở độ phân giải thấp hơn hẳn, có giai đoạn chỉ dừng ở 720p dù máy và mạng đều đủ điều kiện phát 4K.
Vì sao Chrome bị giới hạn suốt nhiều năm
Nguyên nhân nằm ở công nghệ chống sao chép nội dung (DRM). Netflix yêu cầu nội dung Ultra HD phải được giải mã qua một đường dẫn được bảo vệ ở cấp phần cứng, không chỉ bằng phần mềm.
Trên máy tính, Chrome dùng Widevine, công nghệ DRM do chính Google phát triển. Widevine có 3 mức bảo mật, trong đó mức cao nhất (L1) xử lý và giải mã video trong một môi trường phần cứng cách ly, còn mức thấp nhất (L3) xử lý hoàn toàn bằng phần mềm. Vấn đề là phiên bản Chrome chạy trên Windows và macOS xưa nay chỉ đạt L3, nên Netflix coi đây là mức bảo mật chưa đủ để phát Ultra HD.
Ngược lại, Microsoft Edge trên Windows dùng PlayReady, công nghệ DRM của chính Microsoft, tích hợp sâu vào hệ điều hành. PlayReady tận dụng được phần cứng bảo mật sẵn có trong Windows để đạt mức bảo vệ cao hơn, nên Netflix cho phép Edge phát 4K từ lâu.
Theo phân tích kỹ thuật ban đầu, cách Chrome vượt qua giới hạn lần này không phải do Google nâng cấp Widevine lên mức bảo mật cao nhất. Một bản ghi kiểm tra từ phiên bản thử nghiệm Chrome 150 cho thấy trình duyệt này kết nối trực tiếp vào chính hạ tầng PlayReady sẵn có của Windows, thông qua cơ chế Encrypted Media Extensions và Windows Media Foundation, thay vì tự xử lý toàn bộ bằng Widevine. Nói cách khác, Chrome đang mượn con đường mà Edge vẫn dùng, chứ chưa hẳn tự mình đạt chuẩn bảo mật phần cứng.
Những điều kiện cần có để thực sự xem được 4K
Cài Chrome mới nhất không đồng nghĩa với việc Netflix tự động phát 4K. Netflix liệt kê một loạt điều kiện đi kèm.
Máy phải chạy Windows 11 đã cập nhật đầy đủ, Windows 10 chưa nằm trong danh sách hỗ trợ. Tài khoản phải đăng ký gói Premium, gói duy nhất có Ultra HD. Cài đặt chất lượng phát trong Netflix cần đặt Auto hoặc High. Card đồ họa phải đủ mới, tối thiểu Nvidia GeForce GTX 1050, AMD Radeon RX 400 series, hoặc vi xử lý Intel, AMD đời gần đây. Một số máy còn cần cài thêm gói giải mã HEVC Video Extensions của Microsoft. Màn hình phải đạt chuẩn 4K, tần số quét 60Hz, và hỗ trợ HDCP 2.2 trên toàn bộ đường tín hiệu, từ cổng xuất, cáp cho tới màn hình. Nếu máy đang cắm thêm một màn hình phụ không đạt chuẩn, Netflix có thể chặn 4K dù màn hình chính đã đủ điều kiện. Kết nối mạng cần ổn định từ 15 Mbps trở lên.
Ngay cả khi đáp ứng đủ mọi điều kiện, trải nghiệm trên Chrome vẫn chưa trọn vẹn. Netflix chưa mở HDR, Dolby Vision, HDR10+ hay Dolby Atmos cho Chrome, những định dạng hình ảnh và âm thanh này vẫn chỉ dành riêng cho Edge hoặc app Netflix trên Windows.
Còn các trình duyệt khác thì sao
Thay đổi lần này chỉ áp dụng cho Chrome trên Windows 11, không phải một cuộc mở khóa DRM trên diện rộng.
Trên cùng hệ điều hành Windows, Microsoft Edge vẫn giữ lợi thế cũ, không chỉ phát được 4K mà còn có thêm HDR và Dolby Atmos. Firefox và Opera trên Windows hiện vẫn dừng ở 1080p, chưa được Netflix nâng lên 4K như Chrome.
Trên máy Mac, câu chuyện đảo ngược. Chrome chạy trên macOS vẫn bị giới hạn 1080p như trước, người dùng Mac muốn xem 4K vẫn phải mở Safari, trình duyệt duy nhất trên macOS tận dụng được FairPlay, công nghệ DRM riêng của Apple có hỗ trợ phần cứng trên chip Apple Silicon.
Trên Linux, mọi trình duyệt phổ biến đều bị giới hạn thấp hơn hẳn. Chrome, Firefox và Edge trên Linux chỉ đạt tối đa 720p, riêng Opera nhỉnh hơn một chút ở mức 1080p.
Netflix cũng mở thêm hỗ trợ 4K qua Chrome cho một số mẫu Chromebook đạt chuẩn phần cứng riêng, nhưng đây vẫn là nhóm thiết bị hẹp hơn nhiều so với máy tính Windows phổ thông.
Ai ở Việt Nam thực sự dùng được
Tại Việt Nam, gói Premium, gói duy nhất mở khóa Ultra HD, hiện có giá từ 260.000 đến 273.000 đồng mỗi tháng tùy thời điểm, cao hơn hẳn gói Standard chỉ dừng ở Full HD với giá khoảng 220.000 đồng. Với phần lớn người dùng Netflix tại Việt Nam vẫn quen xem qua Smart TV hoặc điện thoại, nhóm hưởng lợi trực tiếp từ thay đổi này là những ai dùng laptop hoặc PC Windows 11 làm màn hình chính, hoặc cắm thẳng máy tính vào TV, màn hình 4K.
Đến thời điểm hiện tại, Google và Netflix đều chưa đưa ra thông báo chính thức nào về thay đổi này. Toàn bộ thông tin đến từ việc người dùng phát hiện trang hỗ trợ của Netflix bị cập nhật âm thầm, cùng một vài bản ghi kiểm tra kỹ thuật độc lập.

articles.title: DeepMind Says Its AI Can Predict Hurricanes Earlier Than Everyone Else
articles.text:
In October 2025, a storm brewed over the Caribbean Sea. Weather models differed on its trajectory. Would it remain weak and end up in Haiti, or would it intensify and head to Jamaica? Artificial intelligence model WeatherNext, developed by Google’s DeepMind and Google Research, went with the latter. Five days before landfall, it predicted with 80 percent confidence that the storm system would hit Jamaica as a Category 5 hurricane.
Hurricane Melissa was catastrophic, causing flooding and landslides across Jamaica. But the AI model helped forecasters give an earlier warning to communities in its path, so they could better prepare.
In a paper published on Thursday in Nature, researchers show that the WeatherNext AI model can predict cyclones with unprecedented accuracy. On average, it gives forecasters a day more lead time than existing models; this means its predictions three days out are as accurate as previous models’ predictions two days out. On the ground, that extra day can mean a lot.
“Even a few hours can make a difference,” says Mike Brennan, director of the US National Hurricane Center. Organizing evacuations, staging supplies, and moving resources to respond to a hurricane risk are all time-sensitive tasks—and making the wrong decision can have big consequences. “Time is really golden when it comes to those types of decisions, so the ability to push forecast accuracy out as much as a day beyond what we've previously been able to do is really valuable,” he says.
Historically, bringing forecasts forward by a day would take a decade of work, the researchers say.
Modeling extreme events can be challenging for AI. Machine learning requires ample training data in order to make future predictions, but extreme events are by nature rare occurrences. “We don’t have that much cyclone data, but we have a lot of weather data,” says Ferran Alet, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and one of the paper’s lead authors. “So what we did was train a model to be both good at weather as well as cyclones.”
Hurricanes are particularly difficult to predict because they operate at multiple spatial scales, says Kate Musgrave, tropical cyclone group lead at the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere, and an author on the paper. Predicting a storm’s track—which direction it’s traveling—requires data about weather on a global scale, taking in information such as the location of cold fronts and prevailing winds. Predicting a storm’s intensity, however, requires much smaller-scale data focused specifically on the local atmospheric and ocean conditions.
“That’s something we just don’t get from these global models,” Musgrave says. While earlier AI models have done well at predicting a storm’s track, “intensity they could not do well at all.”
It’s critical to predict both: A change in intensity can mean the difference between a relatively weak storm and a major hurricane. Sometimes—as in the case of Hurricane Melissa—a storm system can intensify rapidly, developing into an emergency situation overnight. Melissa marked the first time the National Hurricane Centre was able to predict a Category 5 hurricane when the storm was only at a Category 1 stage.
Before the WeatherNext model was used in live forecasts, researchers tested it on retrospective data. “The results were so good that we were skeptical that we would actually see that in the real-time demonstration,” Musgrave says. But when forecasters started adopting the model into their operations, this performance held true. “I think everybody was surprised at just how well it did,” Musgrave says.
Even the DeepMind researchers working on the model don’t fully understand how the AI model produces such accurate predictions, given that it uses much lower-resolution atmospheric data than traditional models require to forecast storm intensity. “When we told the community that our model was only using relatively coarse resolution, they were shocked, because that means that the lower-resolution inputs capture more signal about what’s going to happen than previously believed,” Alet says.
The AI model must be picking up on something in the lower-resolution data that allows it to make predictions about storm intensity, but the researchers don’t know what. “It’s a black box at the end of the day, but that gives physicists a signal that something is happening that was not previously understood,” Alet says.
The model doesn’t just spit out one prediction; it produces a range of potential scenarios for a developing storm. This helps to capture any potential “butterfly effect,” says Alet, where a small deviation from a trend could lead to much bigger changes down the line. Forecasters can use these outputs, alongside those of other models, to inform their predictions about how a storm system will likely unfold. Last year, the AI model created 50 scenarios per storm; now, it generates 1,000.
“That’s something that, with our computing power, we simply can’t do with our existing numerical models,” Musgrave says.
Brennan says DeepMind’s model is a great new tool in forecasters’ toolbox but emphasizes that it’s one of many. “There’s no guarantee that one model, because it did well last year or really did well for this particular storm, is necessarily going to be the best model for the next season or the next storm,” he says. The human element, he adds, is still critical. “A hurricane is not just a track or an intensity forecast,” he says. “It requires experts to translate that into what the impacts are going to be—and it's the impacts that kill people.”
Google DeepMind also announced that it is open-sourcing the WeatherNext models used during hurricane season so that researchers can use and improve on them. Alet is hopeful that opening the models up to the research community could help uncover fresh insights into how cyclones work.
“I’m very excited about scientific discovery,” he says. “I think AI is giving us new tools to poke into the laws of the universe.”

articles.title: Cuối cùng Chrome cũng xem được Netflix 4K, nhưng không phải máy tính nào cũng được hỗ trợ
articles.text:
Netflix đã mở rộng hỗ trợ phát video 4K trên Google Chrome, tuy nhiên chỉ một số thiết bị Windows và Chromebook đủ điều kiện mới có thể sử dụng tính năng này.
Sau nhiều năm bị người dùng phàn nàn vì những giới hạn khi xem nội dung chất lượng cao trên trình duyệt, Netflix cuối cùng đã bổ sung khả năng phát video 4K thông qua Google Chrome. Dù vậy, tính năng này vẫn chỉ dành cho một số thiết bị đáp ứng các yêu cầu phần cứng và phần mềm nhất định, thay vì được triển khai rộng rãi trên mọi nền tảng.
Theo trang hỗ trợ vừa được Netflix cập nhật và được FlatPanelsHD phát hiện đầu tiên, dịch vụ hiện đã hỗ trợ phát nội dung ở độ phân giải Ultra HD trên Google Chrome đối với một số thiết bị chạy Windows và Chromebook. Trong khi đó, người dùng Chrome trên các hệ điều hành khác vẫn phải chấp nhận giới hạn về chất lượng hình ảnh.
Cụ thể, phiên bản Chrome trên macOS chỉ hỗ trợ tối đa độ phân giải Full HD, còn người dùng Linux bị giới hạn ở mức HD 720p.
Để xem Netflix ở độ phân giải 4K hoặc Ultra HD trên Chrome dành cho PC, người dùng cần sở hữu máy tính chạy Windows 11, sử dụng bộ xử lý Intel Core thế hệ thứ 7 trở lên hoặc AMD Ryzen. Ngoài ra, hệ thống cũng phải được trang bị GPU Nvidia GeForce GTX 1050 hoặc AMD Radeon RX 400 series trở lên, hỗ trợ chuẩn mã hóa HEVC và cài đặt đầy đủ trình điều khiển mới nhất.
Đối với Chromebook, Netflix chỉ hỗ trợ phát 4K trên các mẫu Chromebook Plus đã được cập nhật lên phiên bản ChromeOS mới nhất.
Không chỉ yêu cầu về cấu hình, người dùng còn phải sử dụng màn hình tích hợp hoặc màn hình ngoài có độ phân giải 4K, tần số quét 60 Hz và hỗ trợ kết nối tương thích chuẩn HDCP 2.2. Ngay cả khi đáp ứng đầy đủ các điều kiện trên, một số tính năng cao cấp như Dolby Vision, HDR10+ hay Dolby Atmos vẫn chỉ khả dụng khi xem thông qua ứng dụng Netflix, thay vì trên trình duyệt Chrome.
Với những người sử dụng nền tảng khác, vẫn tồn tại các lựa chọn thay thế để xem Netflix ở chất lượng cao nhất. Trên macOS, Safari tiếp tục là trình duyệt duy nhất hỗ trợ phát nội dung 4K, trong khi người dùng Windows cũng có thể sử dụng Microsoft Edge để đạt chất lượng hình ảnh tối đa.
Việc Netflix mở rộng hỗ trợ 4K cho Chrome được xem là một bước tiến, nhưng những yêu cầu phần cứng và nền tảng vẫn khiến trải nghiệm của người dùng trở nên khá phức tạp. Trong nhiều năm qua, không ít bài đăng trên Reddit đã phản ánh tình trạng người dùng gặp khó khăn khi tìm cách xem đúng chất lượng 4K mà họ đã trả phí đăng ký. Thậm chí, một số cuộc thảo luận còn dẫn đến việc nhiều người khuyến nghị sử dụng các nguồn phát nội dung không chính thức vì đơn giản và ít rào cản hơn.
Trong khi các cơ chế bảo vệ bản quyền là một trong những nguyên nhân khiến Netflix áp dụng nhiều điều kiện kỹ thuật, thực tế cho thấy người dùng thường ưu tiên những phương thức xem nội dung thuận tiện nhất. Nếu trải nghiệm từ một dịch vụ trả phí trở nên quá phức tạp, không ít người có thể tìm đến các giải pháp thay thế dễ tiếp cận hơn.
Dù vậy, đối với phần lớn người dùng xem Netflix trên TV thông minh hoặc các thiết bị giải mã, những giới hạn này gần như không tồn tại. Việc mở rộng hỗ trợ 4K trên Chrome được kỳ vọng sẽ là bước khởi đầu để Netflix cũng như các nền tảng phát trực tuyến khác tiếp tục đơn giản hóa trải nghiệm xem nội dung trên máy tính trong thời gian tới.

articles.title: There’s No Good Way to Talk About Celebrities and Eating Disorders
articles.text:
Content warning: This piece includes descriptions of eating disorders that may be triggering to some readers.
Viral discourse about celebrity women becoming frighteningly thin has become inescapable on social media.
There are images showing the most shocking evidence of weight loss, “before and after” compilations, and widespread speculation about covert GLP-1 usage. A lot of the conversation is being held under the guise of concern, but experts tell WIRED many of these posts—even if well-intentioned—misinform the public about eating disorders and can even serve as unhealthy inspiration or trigger those in recovery.
The discourse has reached a fever pitch after Ariana Grande released a music video for her new single and album “Petal,” which features her auditioning endlessly for a table of misogynistic male studio executives who urge her to “lose a few [pounds]” and “get some work done.” Nearly every comment on the video expresses concern for Grande’s health because of her thin appearance. Other celebrities like Jameela Jamil have spoken up, writing that the video was irresponsible for glamorizing a “deeply damaging image for her young fans.”
Following the public reaction to the video, Grande’s team announced that she would be pulling out of a planned theatrical run on London’s West End and “taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny” after she wraps up her Eternal Sunshine Tour. But that statement prompted even more critical discourse, with commenters arguing that they were being villainized for caring about the pop star’s health and influence.
It’s understandable why people are concerned, both for and about Grande.
The renaissance of the unhealthy “heroin chic” beauty standard, following the rise and apparent fall of “body positivity” in the 2010s, coincided with an alarming increase in the number of young people seeking treatment for eating disorders, which can be life-threatening.
Posting about eating disorders—celebrity or otherwise—can be an earnest attempt to save people from them. Images that highlight Grande’s thinness have become unavoidable, though, even for people who are actively trying to avoid being triggered by them. Their ubiquity is exacerbated by social media algorithms that show people increasingly extreme rabbit holes of the same kind of content they previously engaged with.
“I feel pretty comfortable saying that sharing these specific images of [Grande], including ‘before and afters,’ is both unhelpful and harmful,” says Allison Logue, a family therapist with a decade of experience treating patients with eating disorders. She said that sharing comparison pictures is common among people with eating disorders. Some of the viral posts about celebrity women’s appearances are indistinguishable or even come directly from pro-anorexia or “pro-ana” spaces where at-risk individuals use them as inspiration and to compete with each other for a similar appearance.
When celebrities receive an outpouring of attention based on their weight loss, it may encourage some individuals with eating disorders to try to imitate that appearance and seek out that same concern, Logue adds. The broad obsession with celebrities’ weight also reinforces the idea that everyone is paying attention to and judging how you look, which can exacerbate the fears of people with eating disorders.
While Logue told WIRED that Grande’s appearance is concerning—and has been for years—she says that as a stranger, she cannot say for sure whether Grande is struggling with an eating disorder. She notes that the media’s overwhelming focus on individuals with lower weights obscures the reality that people of any and all sizes can have eating disorders.
When a patient is seeking treatment, Logue says, she does not use their appearance to express concern or as a motivator, because there are always other contributing factors. With a public figure, Logue says, we don’t have real insights into these factors. Instead, most people focus on what their body looks like.
Although a lot of commenters say they’re less worried about Grande individually and more concerned about the impact she may have on her young fans, Logue says focusing our efforts on celebrities’ appearances also doesn’t meaningfully combat aspirational thinness in our day-to-day lives, either.
“Talking about how you look fat, engaging in fatphobia, it’s all these things that are so normalized. And when I work with clients, that is the dangerous stuff,” she says. “I’ve never had a client sit down and say, ‘I got an eating disorder because I heard Demi Lovato had an eating disorder.’”
One big sign that the viral posts about celebrities aren’t helping people with eating disorders is that almost none of them share resources, such as links to groups like the National Eating Disorder Association. And many of the posts contain an undeniable strain of snark, cruelty, and carelessness. There are viral compilations of celebrity women with captions like “it’s not just Ariana,” most of which exclude celebrity men entirely. Some people have used AI tools to edit images of these women to make them appear obese and used them as memes, while others have analyzed every part of their bodies in photos to declare them too skinny.
Women in various stages of eating disorder recovery are actively grappling with the issue. Natália Franz, a Slovak actress, commented on one video about celebrities and eating disorders to say, “I wish more people were worried about me when I was not eating rather than normalizing it.”
Franz tells WIRED that she’s concerned about the influence celebrities have over their fans, and she’s hoping that the discourse can change the culture for her own daughter. She also says that her body image issues started at home and that parents need to be careful with how they talk about food and appearance around their kids.
“I actually think it's weird this heated discussion is only about one celebrity,” Franz says. “But when you see so many celebrities getting this thin, it’s very obvious patriarchy is on the rise.”
Having a personal history with eating disorders can provide a more informed perspective, as evidenced by some of the more nuanced conversations happening online. But the reality is that eating disorders are complicated, multifaceted, and different from person to person. Outsiders cannot infer what is going on privately in any celebrity’s life based on the limited information they share with the public, but that doesn’t stop people from labeling those in their inner circle “enablers” or assuming that a break from the public eye means they’re seeking treatment for an eating disorder.
“Talking about this in a heightened, gossipy, fearmongering kind of way is not necessarily going to inspire people to get help,” says Keesha Amezcua, chief clinical officer at Alsana Eating Disorder Treatment Center. “A lot of people on social media platforms are not informed, they’re not educated, and they don’t know what they’re witnessing and participating in is incredibly unhealthy and harmful.”
The National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline provides resources about treatment options at 1-866-662-1235, or you can text “ALLIANCE” to 741741 if you are experiencing a crisis. More information can be found on the National Eating Disorder Association’s website.
